speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   AUDITOR GENERAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was very interesting to hear what was said in the House about when, and especially how, the Auditor General should report the results of his audits. Mr. Speaker, as you know, I myself had some problems with the tabling of certain investigations by the Auditor General, but on the whole, I would say that in 1980, the previous Government, lethargic though it was, supported the Public Accounts Committee which had recommended that the Auditor General report more frequently.

July 18, 1988
Auditor General Act
Between 1980 and 1984, nothing happened, owing to the lethargy of the previous Government, as I just said.
Since then, however, our Government made recommendations in 1984, in 1986 and even this year, in 1988, to improve the situation. We are not afraid of the Public Accounts Committee or the Auditor General's reports. In fact we support them. However, the Auditor General himself, Mr. Kennet Dye, recommended on several occasions that the Auditor General's Act should be amended to allow him to report immediately on certain specific audits, right after completion. He made the point that this would speed up work in his office and improve efficiency. At various times, all parties represented in this House supported at least the principle that amendments were necessary to authorize the Auditor General to report more frequently and on a completion basis.
The reasons in favor of such changes were that tabling of reports immediately upon completion of audits would give the Public Accounts Committee and parliamentarians a better chance to discuss the issues involved while they were still very current and thus corrective action could be taken far more quickly and more effectively.
I would like to point out that the purpose of this Bill is not to table reports on very urgent matters. The Auditor General may at any time make such reports, Mr. Speaker. There is no limitation on the subject matter of such reports. Today, however, we are talking about questions that are not judged by the Public Accounts Committee to be of vital importance or extremely urgent.
It is claimed that this change advocated by this Bill would have the advantage that the public servants called to testify before the Public Accounts Committee would more likely be those involved when the Auditor General made his observations. That is true, Mr. Speaker. However, I sincerely do not believe that the turnover is significant enough for this Bill to apply, It is believed that all these changes will make the Government more accountable to Parliament and thereby to the taxpayers, which is an objective that we all support.
Nevertheless, it is obvious that in spite of the support expressed for changes that at first seem simple and uncomplicated, there has not been unanimous support in this House for the changes proposed to the Auditor General Act. As with many issues brought up in this House, I believe that this question is more complex, much more complicated than people seem to think. Personally, I see some negative effects that could result from it and far outweigh the advantages described.
As I see it, the question we must really ask is what the impact of these changes will be on the Auditor General's effectiveness. I would not want to support changes that would in any way compromise the effectiveness of the Auditor General's Office by imposing on him a host of complications that would make his work more difficult.
The issue of the efficiency with which the Auditor General's Office can produce its reports is in reality secondary. The cost is relatively insignificant compared to the fantastic savings that result from the Auditor General's work. We would not want to compromise his effectiveness for relatively unimportant savings. It has been recognized for a long time that the Auditor General should have the resources he needs to do his job effectively and freely.
Mr. Speaker, in my mind there is no doubt that the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee do important work. In fact, when this matter was discussed in the House last October, the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) pointed out quite rightly that the Auditor General's findings have become more encouraging and that he recognizes that progress has been made in solving the problems described in previous reports. Mr. Speaker, it clearly follows that our Government is responding well to the recommendations of the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee. And before anyone accuses me of being partisan-I certainly am not and I hope I did not give that impression-I think Hon. Members should compare the present tone of the reports to those tabled in the early eighties.
Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General has never been as laudatory in his comments as he has been since this Government came to power in 1984. Previously, the Auditor General's reports were a catastrophe for all Canadians. Our policies have been revamped, and we welcome his reports instead of hiding from reporters when the reports are tabled, which was the case between 1980 and 1984, Mr. Speaker.
I think the system works very well, and in fact it is improving, and that is what we are here for. I agree that completion-based reporting would make it possible to obtain the conclusions several months earlier. However, that alone would not resolve the problem of timeless, if there is such a problem. It is a fact that in many cases, carrying out a comprehensive audit within a department may take up to two years.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, in Parliament and in the departments, we welcome the Auditor General's comments which make it possible for us to improve the situation as we go along, without having to wait for the final results several years later. Mr. Speaker, this new approach to government is that of a businessman who has been involved in politics and not of politicians who think they can do business, as was the case with the previous Government.
We must not forget that audit results are discussed with management as they are drafted. In government, managers must deal with problems on a priority basis as soon as they are brought to their attention. They cannot wait until the final report. Corrective action is generally taken well before the annual report is tabled.
Mr. Speaker, this is a new approach. It is ongoing management and no longer disaster management as was the case before.
July 18, 1988

Under the new system of increased departmental authority and responsibility established by Treasury Board, ministers and senior officals are even more strictly accountable for the measures they take to correct deficiencies in the management of taxpayers' money, and for doing so as they are detected, instead of letting them go on for a couple of years and waiting until the final report to apologize for past mistakes, after officials have left or politicians have been replaced. That was the old way which our businessmen's government cannot accept.
There already are mechanisms to ensure that attention is given quickly to matters of a pressing nature raised by the Auditor General. In fact, the Auditor General, as I said earlier, already has the authority to bring urgent questions to the attention of the House, and to do so at any time. He is not prohibited from speaking out before he tables his final report. He may, at any time, draw the attention of the Prime Minister and Parliament to any matter he deems appropriate.
Mr. Speaker, I believe nevertheless that it may not be advisable to table audit results automatically, upon completion. It is reasonable to suppose that the Auditor General would be given a short-term investigative function that could be used to fuel the controversies of the day. The risk would increase if Bill C-271, allowing standing committees to ask the Auditor General to examine specific questions, were adopted. The Auditor General might then have to investigate some questions that would impede him in carrying out his heavy responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General must still have the right to choose what he considers pertinent to investigate and not simply accede to all the frivolous requests from sensationseeking Opposition parties.
Mr. Speaker, we have a high quality audit bureau that reports to Parliament and it seems to me that we should look very closely at the consequences of the proposed changes to the Auditor General Act before implementing them. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this Bill is unacceptable because of the lack of measures in it to preserve the Auditor General's independence.
Mr. Speaker, in this whole matter, we must judge the operations of the Auditor General on the basis of the powers conferred by our party since we took power and the responses we make to the deficiencies that he has discovered in our system. We do not wait four or five years or two years or for an election before realizing that things are not right. We correct them as we go along and we intend to continue to do so like the good businessmen we have always been.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (for the Minister of the Environment) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act and to amend an Act to amend the National Parks Act, be read the third time and passed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

July 18, 1988
National Parks Act

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) supports this Bill very enthusiastically, as he does everything I do in the Government and in the National Capital Region. He is a great credit to this region. He is going to work for me in the next election.
I am pleased to have been chosen to speak on behalf of the Government on this extremely important and timely piece of environmental legislation. As you know, Sir, I am one of the legislative committee chairpersons and I have a personal policy of not wanting to get involved in debates on any Bill I had chaired or was going to chair. However, as a former National Parks employee I am making an exception because I am intensely proud of that past and our expanding National Parks system. Also, the legislative committee proceeded in a very non-partisan way on what we all agree is a very non-partisan but important national issue.
A short time ago the Canadian Environment Protection Act was the first comprehensive federal environmental legislation in this country's history to be passed by Parliament. On behalf of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and his Parliamentary Secretary, I have the honour of speaking to another tremendously significant environmental initiative as it comes before this House for third reading, namely, the long overdue amendments to the National Parks Act.
In 1974 the Act was amended in a minor way. The Act which was originally created in 1930 by this Parliament is now being amended in a significant way, 58 years after it first came before this House.
The Environmental Protection Act is aimed at safeguarding us in our homes, our businesses, our industries, and our urban areas. In short, it protects the people of Canada where we live and work.
The National Parks Act is aimed at safeguarding special islands in an urban sea for the times we leave our normal surroundings and wish to revive our spirits-places where we surrender control and manipulation of our environment and let nature itself dictate the terms of our visit.
I am sure you will agree, Sir, that we all need and deserve clean, unpolluted surroundings for the enjoyment of our everyday lives. We need and deserve the refreshment of nature when we depart from our routines. This is what the quality of life in Canada is all about. How many times have you told yourself that you want to get away to somewhere quiet, somewhere clean?
Canada is often called the country of the great white north. God bless the great white north. Let us keep it strong and free. These revisions to the National Parks Act will significantly enhance those opportunities, not only for our people but for those around the world who visit our great system.
CEPA and the National Parks Act will work side by side to keep the quality of life in Canada one of the highest in the world. In the case of the national parks, even those unfortunate people who have never visited one must take pride that this nation has the sensitivity to preserve such magnificent examples of our national heritage. Last year over 19 million individuals, mostly Canadians, visited the national parks system in our country.
The National Parks Act amendments are strong simply because they must be strong. It is a great credit to the legislative committee members who reviewed Bill C-30 that they recognized this need and worked long and hard to reshape and add to the original proposals. I commend the opposition Members on the committee whose reasoned analyses of the issues led to many important changes being adopted in the report.
Over 30 individuals and groups who made consistently thoughtful and insightful oral or written presentations on behalf of their specific interests are also to be commended for their input to Bill C-30.
Participation ranged from environmental organizations such as the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society-and here I wish to congratulate Kevin McNamee, the conservation director for that society, for the tremendous work that he and his society did toward helping us making this a better Bill-to groups representing the native peoples of Canada and tourism-oriented agencies such as the Chamber of Commerce in Jasper.
All of their very thoughtful presentations included some suggested changes to the Bill. We could not accept all of them, but we certainly satisfied many of the requests they brought forward to make it a stronger and better Bill. Through that process of consultation, this committee can be very proud of the work it did.
One of the most significant changes to the original Bill concerns the addition of the legislated requirement to produce management plans for each national park. It was evident from the committee hearings that the wide range of viewpoints and the passionate concerns of interest groups must inescapably be considered in preparing such plans. The parks service has a very good record in conducting consultation, but the committee decided that a greater accountability was needed.
The committee therefore proposed that all plans be tabled in the House, that such plans be reviewed every five years and retabled in the House with any changes. That proposal was accepted. Through that process of consultation, the framework of the actual purpose of the national parks which is outlined in Clause 4 can and will be maintained clearly and consistently. Clause 4 states:
The National Parks of Canada are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment... and shall be

July 18, 1988

maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.
It reminds me of when I worked in Africa at the national parks in Tanzania. The sign at the entrance of the Serengeti National Park read: "Here the world is still young and fragile, held in trust for your sons and ours". We can apply a similar philosophy to the national parks in our great country.
A significant amendment that was accepted by the committee was put forward by the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). It links directly to the importance of having those management plans tabled and approved in Parliament. His amendment read:
Maintenance of ecological integrity through the protection of natural resources shall be the first priority when considering park zoning and visitor use in a management plan.
Another important amendment states that the Minister of the Environment will table a document in the House every two years reporting on the state of the parks and progress toward establishing new parks.
Other changes made as a result of the process of consultation on Bill C-30 relate to the additional protection in a second schedule of certain wildlife species. We also incorporated at report stage reference to national marine parks, the first one being on the Bruce Peninsula in Ontario.
This new national marine park reference signals the start of an ambitious program of conservation aimed at protecting significant examples of the salt and freshwater environments.
The Minister will use this new found authority to push on with important initiatives related to establishing marine parks in South Moresby, the Saguenay and many other parts of Canada.
Another provision of the Bill which has been requested since the first Act was proclaimed in 1930 is the change to penalty provisions that were drastically out of date. Bill C-30 has now established the highest fines in the world for the protection of endangered and trophy species in our national parks. For example, fines of up to $150,000 can now result from convictions of those killing threatened species such as polar bear and bighorn sheep. Fines could be up to $10,000 for persons convicted of killing protected species such as wolf or elk in our national parks.
In order for the parks employees to enforce these new measures of protection, they will need more help from the Ministry of the Environment. I encourage the Government and the Minister to allocate the help that the enforcement officers will need to catch those who are destroying our wildlife.
Bill C-30 will also ensure continued protection for wilderness areas. Within Banff and Jasper National Parks in particular, it will give a clear rationale for defining limits to commercial and urban development.
Aside from the Bruce Peninsula National Park and the National Marine Park amendments introduced at report stage,
National Parks Act
Bill C-30 will establish Ellesmere Island National Park Reserve and give proclamation authority for Grasslands National Park in Saskatchewan.
I am proud to be speaking on behalf of the Government. I congratulate the Minister and, particularly his Parliamentary Secretary who worked long and hard and showed excellent leadership in ensuring that Bill C-30 has come to pass. The committee did an excellent job. Most important, the officials and the staff who helped us throughout our deliberations did a superb job. I congratulate all of them.
Parliament will have its final say on behalf of our people and our parks. This is a very proud moment for me because I first went to our national parks system as a labourer. Now I am speaking as a legislator.
In 1967, when I went to Banff National Park to work as a labourer, I recognized the magnificence and beauty of that park. I know the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is proud to say that that part of his wonderful province has been entrenched in law for over 100 years. I recall that Jack Nicol was director general of Parks Canada and Jean Chretien was Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development at that time. I give him credit for initiating new national parks during his mandate.
Pierre Lesaux, presently one of the commissioners at the Public Service Commission of Canada, worked for the parks system. Pierre Desmeules was involved in the resource inventory task force. All of us worked hard to make sure that our parks systems would continue to grow.
It is my honour, looking back over 21 years of national parks interest, service and dedication, to have this last word before our National Parks Act is amended and greatly strengthened by this Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act. First, I want to congratulate my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for the excellent work he has done in this area. We know that the Member was an excellent Minister of the Environment and is someone who really cares about environmental issues. Unfortunately, he cannot be with us today because he is representing our country at an international conference on environmental issues. Again, he has our interest at heart.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) described this Bill as a major piece of legislation. While our national parks system is a major issue, this legislation itself does not qualify as the type of legislation described by the Member for Ottawa-Carleton. After all, this is a Bill that was introduced in a previous Parliament, by the Hon. Member for Davenport when he was Minister of the Environment. Since the previous Parliament dissolved in July, 1984, one wonders why the new Minister of the Environment waited until December, 1986, to reintroduce what is essentially the

July 18, 1988
National Parks Act
same Bill. One cannot help but wonder why the Bill was allowed to gather dust all that time. Nevertheless, the Hon. Member for Davenport and I are very pleased the Bill is proceeding now. After all, it was a Bill he introduced.
As I indicated moments ago, the Bill was introduced in this House in December of 1986. One would have assumed the Government would have dealt with it expeditiously, trying to advance the legislation and make progress so that it could wind its way through the different processes. However, interestingly enough, the Bill which has just been described as landmark and super important by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton was not even touched by the Government for 16 months. Sixteen months after it was introduced in the House in December of 1986, remembering that it had gathered dust for 30 months before that, the Government began to proceed with second reading debate.
During those 16 months there were urgings by Members of this House, particularly the Hon. Member for Davenport, that the legislation proceed and be enacted into law. Nevertheless, there was a considerable delay. One could ask why there was a delay. According to the Edmonton Journal of December 5, 1987, Bill C-30 was "held hostage by the Tory Alberta caucus". The ransom demanded for allowing Bill C-30 to go through Parliament was the expansion of tourism and resource development in national parks, particularly the four mountain parks in British Columbia and Alberta. Those, of course, are Yoho, Banff, Jasper and Waterton.
According to R.V. Rasmussen of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society in Edmonton, the Minister of the Environment had the people of Alberta on his side. In a letter dated January 10, 1988, to all Members of Parliament, Mr. Rasmussen wrote:
The Alberta caucus is very much out of touch with Albertans on this issue.
I have a copy of that letter in front of me, in fact.
Letters and editorials are unanimously against the development stance. In
fact, there has not been a single letter (to the editor) supporting the stance
of the Alberta caucus.
With the public on his side, we all hoped that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. MacMillan) would stand up to some of those Members of Parliament, and I do not know whether the Member opposite is one of them. I can only report the information we received from the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society. Instead, the Minister retreated. He supported the removal of the boundaries of the Sunshine Valley Ski Village from Bill C-30 instead of leaving it to Cabinet to decide on the degree of expansion to allow for the ski area.
In other words, the original proposal would have called for Parliament to decide on the boundaries of this particular ski village. That decision can now be taken by Cabinet. We feel this was a watering down of what otherwise could have been stronger legislation. This was the price the Minister agreed to
pay in order to get the co-operation of some of his colleagues in getting Bill C-30 through Parliament.
I would like to speak briefly about the improvements to Bill C-30. Witnesses in front of the legislative committee put forward some excellent suggestions to improve the Bill. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton has referred to some of those. The committee accepted a number of amendments proposed by the Hon. Member for Davenport and others to make Bill C-30 a better piece of legislation. The Canadian Heritage Fund was dropped. This scheme proposed to solicit money from individual Canadians to improve national parks, but the fund would be spent at the direction and discretion of the Minister. There had been no consultation with nongovernment groups who were seen as the instruments to collect the money for what appeared to be little more than funds that could be used for political motives.
Fortunately, the committee was convinced to remove this measure from the Bill and we urge the Minister of the Environment to take up the offer of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society and immediately initiate discussions with all interested parties to determine how best to set up a cooperative funding scheme that would be acceptable to all parties concerned and, most important, lead to the development of a capital fund for the acquisition of new parks in Canada.
Ecological principles will be made the first management priority for national parks as a result of an amendment to Bill C-30. This important amendment was suggested by the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society so that the National Parks Act would reflect the principles laid out in the 1979 Parks Canada policy. Believe it or not, Mr. Speaker, government members on the committee initially refused to support this amendment which legislated parks policy until interventions were made by interested parties. In other words, government members refused to go along with this proposed amendment.
Overnight, a number of people, particularly the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, lobbied and convinced the Minister that this amendment was worth while. Overnight the officials of the Department redrafted the same amendment- with a few different words, of course-and when government members came into the committee room the next day, and looked at the brand new amendment, they noted how much better it was than the previous one. Of course, it was exactly the same but with different words. The amendment passed unanimously.
Another amendment adopted by the committee will require the Minister to prepare and table in the House a park management plan for new parks within five years of their proclamation. There is now also a requirement for public participation in the preparation of management plans, as appropriate.
The Minister will also be required to report to Parliament every two years on the status of the national parks system and the progress made toward establishing new parks. That again
July 18, 1988

was referred to previously today by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton.
We all know the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton is indeed an expert in this area. As he indicated, he has been a park warden both in this country and abroad. I have often chatted with him about such issues and I can indeed attest to the fact that he is very knowledgeable in the area of the functioning and management of parks.
There are still things missing in Bill C-30. We voted about an hour ago on amendments to Bill C-30 which would have made the legislation far better. The Canadian Landmarks program was approved in principle in 1979 when the present Speaker of our Parliament was Minister of the Environment. The 1984 land claims settlement of the Inuit of the western Arctic established the pingos of Tuktoyaktuk as a Canadian landmark to be managed by the Minister of the Environment under the National Parks Act. For those who are not familiar with "pingos", they are a very unique feature. It is a form of outcrop coming from the land which is caused by heaving. It is similar to what we might find in our driveway in the spring with the exception that they are much higher. I am told they can be 60 to 70 feet high. They are a very unique and distinctive formation. They are indeed something that is very special. They have been identified as a landmark.
The present Act makes no reference to Canadian landmarks, even though there was an amendment proposed to have those landmarks identified. Parks Canada is having some difficulty in finding a way to carry out its mandate with respect to the pingos of Tuktoyaktuk. The Hon. Member for Davenport put forward a motion to include the Canadian landmarks in the Act. The Minister wrote back to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport, saying what a great idea this is. As a matter of fact, I have a copy of a letter undoubtedly written by officials in the Minister's Department. There are a few handwritten notes in which the Minister tells my colleague, the Member for Davenport: "P.S. Charles, you can count on my full support of the idea. I'm eager to pursue it with you. Might we discuss how the program could be launched in a way that will work and that won't violate the fiscal rules to which I am subject..." The Minister of the Environment responded to my colleague, suggesting that it was a neat idea to identify and protect the landmarks. "I am glad you are putting up this amendment. Isn't this great. Don't know what I can do about it, but I am glad you are bringing it up. Why don't we meet and discuss it sometime".
The interesting thing is that Canadian landmarks are already part of the Parks Canada policy. In other words, the Parks Canada policy which governs the Minister's own Department covers the landmarks. Seemingly the Minister did not know about this when he wrote that letter to my colleague.
National Parks Act
I have a copy of "Canadian Landmarks" component of Parks Canada policy. Page 59 of "Canadian Landmarks" states:
Parks Canada Objective for the Canadian Landmarks System. To foster protection for all time of exceptional natural sites of Canadian significance in a co-operative system of Canadian landmarks, and to encourage public understanding and appreciation of this natural heritage so as to leave it unimpaired for future generations.
1.0	Proposed Criteria for Inclusion in the Canadian Landmarks System.
1.1	Canadian landmarks must be exceptional natural sites of Canadian significance identified according to the following criteria:
i)	the sites must contain a natural feature or phenomenon which is unique or rare in Canada or the world, or the sites must be the best example of a particular natural theme component in Canada; and
ii)	the sites must have experienced minimum modification by man or, if such modification has occurred, the main feature must be unaffected and the sites must have potential for restoration to a natural state.
There are pages here describing the landmark system.
You will recall what I just quoted from the handwritten note of the Minister saying what a great idea it is to talk about these landmarks, and what could we do to promote it. One can now attest to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister did not seem to be too much au courant of the policy of his own Department, the policy which is supposed to govern what he does, by the way.
I want to talk briefly about the non-derogation clause. A little earlier this evening we voted on the amendment which was proposed by the Hon. Member for the Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin). The Tungavik Federation of the Nunavut brought to the attention of the committee that there was a potential for conflict between the National Parks Act and Section 35 of the Constitution Act dealing with aboriginal rights. The Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society and the Prairie Treaty Nations Alliance supported and reinforced the submission of the Nunavut. As a result, the offending clause of Bill C-30 was amended. However, Professor Brad Morse of the University of Ottawa Law School pointed out that there could be a conflict between Section 6(1) of the National Parks Act which is not affected by Bill C-30, and section 35 of the Constitution Act. For this reason he suggested that a nonderogation clause be moved at report stage to protect the rights of aboriginal peoples in the event of a conflict between Bill C-30 and the Constitution. That essentially is the amendment that we were voting on tonight as proposed by the Hon. Member for Yukon.
Interestingly enough the Government chose to vote down that amendment. What bothers me is the fact that we pass legislation on a fairly frequent basis relating to resources or lands that contains a clause identical or fairly similar to the one proposed by my Hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Yukon. If the Government states that that one was not appropriately worded, why did it not propose one of its own, so at least the Bill would have contained that non-derogation clause which we should include more and more in legislation,

July 18, 1988
National Parks Act
particularly when we are dealing with resources or with land issues.
Finally, I want to talk about the Sunshine ski area in Banff. I have been to that area. As a matter of fact, like most Canadians, I probably see the national parks in the context of making a short visit to Jasper or Banff, as I did last year. My family and I skied at Sunshine Village. It is a very beautiful area in which to ski. I am sure all Canadians want us as a country to have those facilities in that beautiful setting in Banff. I believe that is in the constituency of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I am sure he must be very proud of that area. It is absolutely beautiful. It was the first time that I visited the Sunshine Village. I am sure the Hon. Member and all his constituents must be very proud of it. Of course, all of us want that type of enterprise to succeed, and we want to attract tourists. We favour the proper development of that type of an area.
There boundaries of the ski area were agreed to in 1979, following a number of years of public consultation. That is the way in which it should be done. There should be public consultation. We must always ensure that the ecological concerns are taken care of before developing or increasing the size of a development. The commitment was made then to legislate these boundaries so that only Parliament could, in its collective wisdom, expand the boundaries of the ski area. It was the reneging of this commitment by the governing Party that resulted in the situation that we now have where Bill C-30 has changed that wherein in the future Cabinet unilaterally can make that type of change. We believe that the Bill would have been far better had the Government stayed the previous course of having that type of change made by the House of Commons.

So, Mr. Speaker, to conclude, we, for our part, support Bill C-30. As 1 indicated earlier, this Bill was delayed by the Government for a very long time. As I said, the Bill was put on the back burner for about two years, and was then introduced to the House and stayed on the shelf for another long while. We, however, do not want to delay the Bill's possible adoption in any way. I do regret, as does my colleague the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) that the Government has decided to amend the Bill with regard to the Sunshine Village Ski Area in Alberta, as I said earlier.
Nevertheless, I support the Bill. The others members of my party intend to support it, and there would be no advantage to delaying this Bill tonight.
I will conclude with that, Mr. Speaker, and I do hope that the House, that Parliament, will pass the Bill shortly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to make a contribution to the closing moments
of the debate on Bill C-30. I want to start by indicating that I, like the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), have a fairly lengthy background in parks but not to the same exotic degree as has the Member for Ottawa-Carleton. He has been involved in parks outside Canada, outside this continent. My experiences are primarily within municipalities and within the Province of Ontario.
I give the Government credit for what it is doing today. It is taking that next step in our growth as a nation, in our understanding of the importance of our wilderness areas and of the important aspects of our history from the point of view of human beings as well as geological and marine to ensure that we provide the necessary protection of our natural environment.
On the one hand it is there for the purposes that we need it for and, second, it is there for all of us, whether we be Canadians or visitors to this country, to enjoy nature at its best. Whether it is parks in or close to the urban settings of this country or parks that are long distances away from people, it is extremely important to do.
I want to speak for a moment about the myth that we so often hear about. I hear it in my constituency. There was a newspaper report this morning talking about an attack on a wilderness park operated in the Province of Ontario by people who basically believe that if we cannot cut it, if we cannot dig it out of the ground, if we cannot sell it, it has no value. That myth has no basis in reality. There are some things that we cannot buy or sell. There are some things that should not be cut, some places that we should not dig up. Part of what Bill C-30 does is provide that protection. It also provides the ability to expand that protection. I will come back to that in a moment.
In terms of the wilderness park, there are some who believe that wilderness parks are only there for an exclusive group, be they physically able or financially able to travel to distant points to access these wilderness parks or the national parks. In terms of a mental attitude just because they do not want to use them does not mean that they are important. They forget that there is another value, the real value about parks in general but wilderness parks specifically. On one hand they operate as a bench-mark. I use the term "bench-mark" because I used to be an employee of the Ontario Department of Highways, as a surveyor. My hon. colleague from Bow River will know of what I speak when I talk about a bench-mark being a point of reference, a point that one can measure up or down. Our wilderness parks provide that. They provide it in an ecological sense, so that we can measure the changes in wildlife, the changes in our vegetation, the impact of acid rain, and any other atmospheric pollutants or water pollution. We can measure it and compare it with what the natural should be. That is one important issue of wilderness parks.
The more trees we cut down, the less oxygen we are producing and the less carbon dioxide is being absorbed. This is becoming more and more crucial every day. We are getting
July 18, 1988

into a crisis point because of the greenhouse effect, because of the attempt by the so-called industrial world, the so-called leaders of the economy of the world who are now encouraging those with rain forests to cut them down, to eradicate them. What we are doing, over time, is destroying life on earth as we know it.
Wilderness parks are an extremely small component of the land mass and the vegetation of this world, not only this country. I am sure that if we put all national parks that exist in Canada today in northwestern Ontario from where I come from, we would barely be able to see them. In fact, they probably would not be any bigger than Lake Superior, one of the largest freshwater lakes in the world. They would disappear. It is not as if we are going out there and destroying the economy of the Rockies or northern Ontario or Atlantic Canada; we are protecting something for the future, and it is extremely important that we continue to do so.
It also provides for those that we share this earth with, those so-called less intelligent beings, and I know there are some who will dispute who the most intelligent is.
The animals are.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
We have done a pretty good job of screwing up the earth. They have not had that chance. As we look at them and see how they operate, we know that the fur bearing creatures and feather creatures are in sync with the environment, whereas man, the so-called intelligent species, seems to go out of his and her way to destroy. In fairness, I think we have to say that most of the blame has to be passed on to the males of history, because they are the ones who made the decisions, the mistakes. We have gone out of our way to destroy what existed and what should exist.
The wilderness parks, the national parks, provide an incubator-again another bench-mark-which on the one hand allows us to see the changes elsewhere but on the other hand ensures that those species that we have come close to eradicating for trophies on walls, for souvenirs, or even for food, have a chance to come back. I think of the buffalo in western Canada. I think of the American eagle in the United States.
The Golden Eagle.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
The Golden Eagle. I think of ducks and the fine work being done by Ducks Unlimited, in the sense of restocking. It is not just ducks, but geese. In the area where I live we had not seen geese for years. Now, thanks to Ducks Unlimited, they have been transplanted and we have a very large flock based close to my place in Thunder Bay. It is great to see them. Wilderness parks provide a place for them to live and survive, to grow, to re-establish their species; for another reason, it is important to set that area aside.
Now we can move on and appreciate one of the amendments that was put forward by the Government at the late stages of report stage debate providing for the marine parks, the water
National Parks Act
component. Whether it is in the County of Bruce or elsewhere, we can take a look at our undersea neighbours, our underwater neighbours, to ensure that their species can be protected.
There are things we would have liked to have seen changed in the Bill to make it better and to make it less sensitive to the commercial instincts which the market-place tends to place on us. Unfortunately, the Government did not see the wisdom of the proposals. We also wanted to ensure that the aboriginal peoples, the first people of this nation, in no way were infringed by any element of this piece of legislation so that nothing in the Bill could take away something that by treaty, by agreement, was made between the Government of Canada and their nation. Again, it is unfortunate that the Government did not feel it appropriate to provide that specific override in the legislation. There will come a time when we will ensure that this legislation is improved that much more. Just as we build a nation we will build and develop our parks. I use the term "develop" very loosely. I am not talking about ski resorts or major commercial entities. I am talking about the development of the boundaries to ensure that there are boundaries and about the protection that is necessary to ensure that sites are protected for as long as we are here and for our children, our grandchildren, our great-grandchildren, and so on.
I want to speak to another specific element of the Bill which provides yet even more growth-the ability for us as a Parliament of Canada and for the Cabinet of the day no matter which Party is the governing one, no matter whether it is this year, 10 years or 20 years from now, to have the power to designate national parks. We did that on Friday for four areas of this country: the rural municipalities of Val Marie and Old Post in the Province of Saskatchewan, the County of Bruce in the Province of Ontario-we have also provided specific reference to marine parks in that case-the District of St. Barb and Humber West in the Province of Newfoundland, and the District of Thunder Bay in which I reside. That one, of course, is appropriate to my area and is of specific interest to myself.
I live at the tip of a mountain range. It is a mountain range in northwestern Ontario but you have to appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that it may not be the same size as the ranges in the neighbourhood of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). This mountain range is called the Nor'westers. It has been a dream for years that that range, which runs along the edge of Lake Superior and stretches down to the Pigeon River where the Voyageurs went from Lake Superior up to Lake of the Woods and into western Canada, could be protected forever from development by declaring it a national or a provincial park. This amendment brought forward by the Government, and I do thank the Government for it, was as a result of an initiative taken by the City of Thunder Bay Parks and Recreation Department.
About six years ago, when I was still there as a park planner, we entered into a master planning process to see

July 18, 1988
National Parks Act
where we should be going in the next 10, 15, or 20 years in parks and recreation planning. An item that came out of that study and an analysis of the needs and wishes of the people of Thunder Bay was the need for a wilderness park type facility along the Nor'westers. The report went to the council and it was recommended that we look at it. The City of Thunder Bay wrote to the legislative committee asking to be heard. It saw Bill C-30 as a part of the process which would allow the City of Thunder Bay at the very least to ensure that at some point should the citizens of Thunder Bay agree with the proposal that they would have the opportunity to be heard. Regretfully the committee decided what it wanted was outside the scope of the Bill and declined to invite them to appear. Because they had raised the matter with the committee on my suggestion, it came to the attention of the Government and through the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Browes) a motion was brought forward which included the District of Thunder Bay in that opportunity. It does not mean that the District of Thunder Bay will get a national park. It may not. At some point, even if the community decides or the community of communities decides to make an approach, the Government may say: "I am sorry, we cannot afford it". But it opens the door for the process to begin.
There are some very good restrictions in the process. The land has to be owned by the Government of Canada. This means that private land holders who exist within the broad stretch do not have to fear that somebody will draw a park boundary line which all of a sudden includes their land, preventing them from doing with their land what they have done with it for years. It requires notification so that people have an opportunity for input. It gives the City of Thunder Bay the opportunity to begin discussions with its neighbours to the south and east, the Fort William Indian Band, with its neighbours to the south and west, the Municipality of Neem-ing, and perhaps even farther away to the Municipality of Paipoonge.
We can now begin to talk about how that could work and whether or not there is agreement to bring forward a specific proposal to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) that is well thought out, well supported with a clear idea of the finances involved, letting the Government of the day react. The ball is now in the court of the parks and recreation department of the City of Thunder Bay. What we have done with Bill C-30 is to make sure that the City of Thunder Bay knows the door is open. It is an important step.
The same thing can apply to Newfoundland, to Saskatchewan, to Bruce County, and elsewhere in Ontario because those places too now have that door open to them. They do not have to worry about how to convince Cabinet to bring in a separate Bill to do this when it has a loaded agenda. If it is four years from now we will be bucking against a possible election with people trying to go home for the summer, maybe! This is a good tool. It really does make it easier for representatives of those four areas to put forward their concepts.
It also does not preclude the powers that be in Thunder Bay from saying: "No, it doesn't make sense. We were wrong. However, we might want to make a deal with the Province of Ontario and turn Sibley Provincial Park, which has the famous sleeping giant, into a national park. Everything is wide open within the District of Thunder Bay as a planning tool. That is extremely important, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank Members for the opportunity to participate at third reading on Bill C-30. I know at least one of my colleagues wants to speak about the proposal for the Grasslands Park in Saskatchewan. Perhaps other Members might want to speak.
We will be supporting this Bill. It is good legislation. It could have been better, but we will have our turn to make it even better at some future date.

Mr. Speaker, I was looking at the Bill and I could only find one small reference in it as it pertains to the Prairies, leaving out the references to Banff, Jasper, Elk Island, and a park in Manitoba.
I want to remind the House that it is now about 15 or 16 years ago that I was invited by the then federal Minister of the day and the provincial Minister of the day to a great ceremony and celebration which was held in the City of Regina. Officials were there from the Provinces of Manitoba and Alberta and the States of Montana and North Dakota.
All the wildlife and naturalist people from western Canada were there. Authors and artists were there. Two or three hundred people attended that celebration because it was the announcement of agreement on the Grasslands National Park. My good friend, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), will appreciate that because he has a lot of grasslands in his riding.
Once that had been accomplished, then all the naysayers took over. Every Government since, provincial and federal, of the three different Parties, have procrastinated, waffled, horsed around, delayed, and found every excuse imaginable to avoid having that park proclaimed and instituted.
On the last page of the Bill, in the second last subclause, I saw the rural municipalities of Val Marie and Old Post in the Province of Saskatchewan are mentioned. Those two municipalities, of course, could be part and parcel of a much larger area which will be the Grasslands National Park. Maybe the coming of another drought and the terrible difficulties that our grain and livestock producers are going through will produce over the next several years some great good, because hundreds of those people have already left the area. There is no doubt that hundreds more will do so. Sad to say, what is left of some of the communities in that area are dying. So I suppose it is somewhat ironic that a large area of the Prairies could be returned to mother nature to turn it back into its natural state. Tens of thousands of acres of marginal or submarginal lands that should never have been farmed or ranched in the first
July 18, 1988

place, but thanks to the Hudson's Bay Company and the CPR and a few others like them, they were settled and farmed.
It has always been next year country in that part of my province, if not my whole province. The grasslands is a heritage fast disappearing in Canada and the U.S., the Soviet Union, and parts of Asia where they have vast tracts of grasslands. Yet in those other parts of the world they have much denser populations. There is a unique opportunity here for Canada, if we move fast enough, to allow nature to restore in its natural habitat and environment a truly great prairie grasslands national park. I know my hon. friend from Saskatoon West has been down in that part of the province a lot of times and he knows something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know it like the back of my hand.

If you have never been there, Mr. Speaker, you should go. It is the kind of area where farsighted people come from. You stand on a small hill and you can see straight ahead for three days.
It is not only a question of preserving the grasslands and the wildlife. I want to list a number of species of wildlife that I came up with in my own amateurish manner. All but a couple of them are endangered species whose natural habitat is the Prairies. They are not going to restore themselves unless we make certain there is a territory for them to do it in.
There is the kit fox, kangaroo rats, prairie dogs, sage grouse, sharp-tailed grouse, prong-horned antelope, and the prairie buffalo. That is not the wood buffalo. The prairie buffalo are the big ones. Even elk. Most people do not know that the elk are not native to the mountains. The elk were and are native to the Prairies and if you ever took the trouble to read the journals of the northwest fur traders and the Hudson's Bay fur traders, the ones who went up the North and South Saskatchewan Rivers in their canoes and rafts and came out above the river valley and on to the Prairies, they talk about the tens of thousands of elk and deer and antelope and buffalo that roamed those Prairies. Yet people are surprised when you mention the word elk in connection with the Prairies. They are native to the Prairies, not the mountains. We forced them up there.
Then we have, would you believe, things like cactus? Would you believe even rattlesnakes? I know we have had trouble with rats and snakes there from time to time. It is like trying to get rid of the Liberals and Tories. I am just teasing my good friend from Bow River.
So we have cactus and rattlesnakes, hawks and eagles, burrowing owls, and a host of wildlife and plants and flowers that were always natural to that area. Over the last 20 to 25 years, Sir, we have allowed that wildlife and that natural growth to be devastated with herbicides and pesticides. We have continued to cultivate submarginal land that should never be cultivated. We have continued to allow it to be overgrazed. If there is any one argument that I have had with ranchers it concerns overgrazing. They would overgraze their land all
National Parks Act
year, through the spring, summer, and fall. They would cut hay off the bottom land and then would come running to the provincial Department of Natural Resources, either in Alberta or Saskatchewan, and demand special permits to shoot the elk and moose and deer that came down into their haystacks. What else were those poor beasts supposed to do? I watched elk being slaughtered up in the Crowsnest Pass country when ranchers got their way and got a special permit. They would even run cattle and sheep and horses up above the timber line and graze the meadows down to nothing. As soon as there was a little bit of snow the wildlife came down and got into the haystacks and the ranchers got permits to slaughter them. That is unforgivable. I have no time or patience for those who run livestock and misuse the vegetation or the wildlife. If they are going to keep domestic animals, they have a responsibility to look after them rather than leaving them to fend for themselves at the expense of the wildlife and, later, the expense of the taxpayers.
We have a great opportunity to allow nature to restore to the state it was in when we came here one of the few grasslands areas left in the world. The Indian people moved with the wildlife. When grass and water was in short supply, the wildlife moved and the Indian people moved with them. The area they left was able to restore itself. This grasslands national park must be big enough to allow an element of that to happen.
The Indian people never took more than what they needed for themselves. The white man, who came mostly from Europe, in order to make a buck failed to conserve. I think my friends opposite cherish the word "conserve". If there is one crime which society as a whole has committed, it is our failure to conserve the national elements of our country and, in this instance, our beloved Prairies.
If I had my way on the issue of proclaiming and developing national parks, and I do not know if my own Party would agree with me, I would not let the private sector in on it at all. I wouldn't mind if they put up a couple or three motels and a couple of the chintzy hotdog stands they have in so many of our parks outside the park border, but beyond that they would not be allowed to do anything else. Their primary purpose is to make some dollars and they, like so many of us, want to make dollars at the expense of the natural environment and the wildlife.
The Queen Charlottes, the grasslands, our streams, Rocky Mountains, and rocks in northern Ontario are things which we have no right to leave in a mess for our children and grandchildren to clean up, if possible. There should be no question about the purposes for a national park for our people and for nature and wildlife. Those who are selfish and thoughtless and oppose this sort of thing should be able to have their say. However, unless they can present an overwhelming case, we must proceed with this anyway.

National Parks Act
I wish to invite all of my colleagues to spend an evening camping on the Prairies and to get up before dawn. They will hear a meadow lark sing and a gopher squeak. They will see some hawks and eagles. They will hear a coyote howling from a hill nearby. They will hear the beat of a sagegrouse or sharptailed grouse. They will watch the beauty of a herd of antelope galloping at speeds up to 60 miles an hour. I invite you, Mr. Speaker, and all my colleagues to experience that. If you do so, I expect that we will get an even bigger and better grasslands national park than we are presently envisaging.
I hope this legislation will allow whoever is governing this country to implement this initiative. We will support it in the hopes that that will be accomplished. I hope that Hon. Members will not think only of the Queen Charlottes, northern Ontario, Atlantic Canada, or northern Canada, as beautiful and as great as they are. The most sadly neglected area has been our Prairie grasslands and there is not much time left for it to be rejuvenated. I hope the present Government and all governments succeeding it will ensure that it it preserved.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to support my colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), in the splendid speech he made on grasslands. His remarks reminded me of the first school district in which I was engaged to teach. I was raised in the hills of Drumheller. Around the hills there is a lot of prairie grassland. However, not as much as there was at Lake McKee.
One morning I got up and looked out of the old granary which was serving as a teacherage. I saw about 15 prairie chickens doing I did not know what. I watched them in fascination. They were going through various movements as if they were in a dance or a drill. That lasted for about 15 or 20 minutes. I have never seen anything like it. I wish I had had a camera to take pictures of those prairie chickens which I believe are now extinct on our Prairies.
They are extinct because we destroyed their habitat and also because they were so patient. I remember a friend of mine taking a shot at a prairie chicken when I was just a boy. He missed but the patient prairie chicken gave him a second chance. It sat there and let him shoot it. That is another reason it is extinct.
I love hunting but I have never shot a duck when it was sitting on the water because the very thought of my friend shooting that helpless prairie chicken which was patient enough to give him a second chance always brought horrors to my mind.
I want to support this matter of the grasslands. They are a beautiful thing. During a terrible flood in the Drumheller Valley a nurse came to help us out with some of the tragedies which were taking place there in 1940.
I took her up to the top of a hill to show her the beautiful view of the Nacmine area which the Hon. Member for Regina
West would know well. You could survey the whole valley. I asked her if she did not think it was a beautiful sight, even though it was flooding. She thought it was weird, not beautiful. I said: "Sister, you do not know what beautiful is". Every hill, every blade of grass is beautiful as far as I am concerned. People ask what we see in the grasslands. I will not try to duplicate what the Hon. Member for Regina West said, but everything he said about the grasslands is true.
As a Member representing Banff, where the first national park was formed in Canada, I want to say a few words about how Bill C-30 affects that area. National parks and protection are synonymous and must be kept that way. The meaning of national parks is protection.
The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) mentioned wilderness areas. I too am very fond of wilderness areas and believe they should be protected in their natural state. National parks exist for people to enjoy wilderness areas. Many people enjoy walking, others enjoy riding horses, while others enjoy driving.
People said in the early 1900s that it would be horrible to let a car enter the Banff National Park. While it may have been necessary to cut down some trees for railway lines and roads, without those roads or railway lines it would have been impossible for hundreds of thousands of people to enjoy the beauties of the national park. Today, some people question the necessity of an airstrip in Banff National Park, which has been there for some 15 or 20 years. It has not killed any animals. It is a safety feature for airplanes that get lost in the mountainous area where weather changes rapidly. It brings people in so that they may enjoy the national park.
I agree that national parks need protection, but I think we have to realize that in order for everyone to enjoy the national park there must be means for them to get there, whether it be by train, by car, by horse, by walking, or even by airplane. That is why I would support keeping the airstrip at Banff National Park.
Recently a vote was held in the townsite of Banff. The people voted by a large majority to have local government. Since its inception, the people of Banff have been governed by a "mayor" living 2,000 miles away, the Minister of the Environment. He has had to contend with municipal problems like sewers, roads, snowdrifts, water lines and so on. The people of Banff have not had the privilege of governing themselves.
Now they will have that opportunity and I want to thank the Minister and his staff, as well as the superintendent in Banff and his staff, the school board and their staff and many others in that area who worked together in order to obtain self government. Some may say that an elected council will operate in a way that is not in harmony with the protection provided by national parks. I do not believe there is anyone more anxious to preserve and protect the national park than the people of Banff who live there. It is their livelihood and their joy. It is their life. Consequently, I am sure that no council in Banff will do anything to hurt the national park.
July 18, 1988

There will be two administrations: The town council and the park administration. I believe the two will work together in harmony to solve any problem that may arise in the interest of protection of national parks.
Some people do not favour tourism, but tourists have made Banff National Park what it is today. We want people to continue to enjoy Banff National Park. This means different things to many people. A skier needs a place to ski, and the ski hills must have competitive facilities to attract the skiers. The Hon. Member mentioned Sunshine Village. It is a wonderful site, and unless those facilities are equal to those found south of the border or in British Columbia, people will not visit.
I agree that national parks means protection. We must also make sure that we provide facilities for the people who visit. I do not want a Coney Island in the town centre of Banff, nor do I think anyone in Banff wants that. However, they want facilities that will attract people and let them enjoy the scenery.
Occasionally Banff has closed off trails and hostels. We must be very careful about that. For instance, Shadow Lake is a place to visit for people who are unable to walk very far. They can travel part way up the mountain by car and walk a mile or two to a beautiful place called Shadow Lake. Many people are unable to walk 12 or 14 miles up a mountain. However, I have seen aged people and crippled children travel the last mile and a half to Shadow Lake where they could see Mount Eisenhower and the beautiful scenery which is thrilling to anyone who sees it. I do not want to deny that to the aged or handicapped who cannot travel far. We should provide those facilities so that they may enjoy the scenery as well.
Many of our youth have visited our hostels in Banff. I have received a mass of letters because one hostel is being closed. The facilities must be competitive as well as in harmony with the parks. The people of Banff are just as anxious to achieve that as anyone else.
I want to say a few words about the people who live in Banff. They often feel like second class citizens who cannot enjoy the same rights under the laws of Canada as Canadians who do not live in a national park. Sometimes this is true.
I recently sent a letter to the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) because civil servants and RCMP in Banff are required to pay rent and live in houses that belong to the Government. The fact is that the rent for houses in Banff is the highest of any park in Canada, some three or four times the rent paid in eastern Canada or central Canada, and twice as much as they pay in Jasper.
National Parks Act
These people are citizens of Canada. Some may say they should save enough to buy a house but there are no houses for sale in Banff. They live in a different community because the national park must be careful about how much land it uses for developing single houses. The rents are excessive, and I have been asking the President of the Treasury Board to consider this problem. These people should not be treated that way, and I think we will solve these (ground rents) through the town council and an arrangement with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). I think that is an essential item as well. Some of the commercial operations are being taxed excessively. They all want to pay their taxes but not in such excessive amounts that they cannot even make a living. These are the things I think we have to look at very carefully.
There are many, many things in Banff that we could talk about which would be interesting and worth while, but I want to say that I have found the people of Banff to be protective oriented. They want to protect the environment, but they also want the same rights as every other Canadian citizen, and I want them to have the same rights as citizens of Calgary, Drumheller or Toronto. They are citizens too. They should not be penalized because they live in a national park.
We want to bring more and more people to these parks. I wish every person in Canada could enjoy the beauty described by our Liberal friend a few moments ago. I want to thank the Members who worked on the National Parks Act, those who are protecting our environment and our habitat and, most of all, making our national parks-and I am thinking of Banff because that is the one in my riding-a place where people love to go and return to again and again because they enjoy the scenery and the excellent facilities.
